title: From Curry Clubs to Beer Gardens: Indian Food Finds Home in English Pubs
excerpt: From village pubs in Worcestershire to London locals hosting Diwali parties, Indian food festivals are drawing crowds to some of England's most traditional drinking spots.
body:
• Indian food festivals and curry nights are increasingly finding a home in traditional English pubs, from Worcestershire villages to London locals.
  • The Great Malvern Food Festival in July 2026 featured Indian savoury and sauce traders among more than 50 stalls in the town's Priory Park.
  • Pub chains have leaned into the trend for years: JD Wetherspoon's Thursday Curry Club has run for over a decade, and London pubs now host Diwali celebrations alongside real ales.
  • Indian restaurants have been part of the Malvern food scene since 1987, when Anupam opened its doors in Great Malvern.

In pubs across England, the smell of cumin and coriander now competes comfortably with hops and malt. What was once a novelty — an Indian food festival in the garden of a traditional English pub — has become a fixture of the summer calendar, drawing crowds that come for the curry and stay for the pint.

The latest example comes from Worcestershire, where the Malvern Gazette reported on an Indian food festival staged at a local pub that blended the two cultures so completely that organisers described it as a meeting of worlds: tandoor smoke drifting over the beer garden, families sharing tables over thalis and ale. It is the kind of event that would have raised eyebrows a generation ago and now barely needs explaining.

A festival in the beer garden

The Malvern area has been building toward this moment for years. The Great Malvern Food Festival, held on July 4 and 5 this year in the town's Priory Park, listed more than 50 traders — including Aunties Sauces, selling Indian savouries and sauces, among the artisan stalls. The free festival has become one of the region's largest, and Indian food has moved from the margins of the trader list to its centre.

That reflects a deeper local history. Anupam, described by the town's visitor guide as Indian dining at its best, has stood in the heart of Great Malvern since 1987. It has since been joined by a cluster of Indian and Nepalese restaurants — Flute Signature and Gurkha Chef on Graham Road, the Lantern Restaurant on Belle Vue Terrace — that have made the town an unlikely stronghold of subcontinental cooking in the English countryside.

The Thursday curry club phenomenon

The pub industry spotted the opportunity long ago. As far back as 2010, JD Wetherspoon staged a week-long curry festival across 64 of its pubs in north-west England, serving ten curries from its regular menu plus guest dishes of lamb chettinadu and Goan chicken curry. Its supplier, the Authentic Food Company, even teamed up with Phoenix Brewery to create a bespoke ale designed to be drunk with curry.

The experiment became permanent. Wetherspoon's Thursday Curry Club — curry, rice, naan, chutney and poppadoms with a drink — has now run for well over a decade, and the company has claimed the title of "the nation's biggest curry house every Thursday night." Independent pubs have gone further: London's Gladstone Arms hosts Indian food events and Diwali parties, pours White Rhino lager brewed in Gwalior, and stocks Indian whiskies behind the bar.

"We also do Indian events, Diwali parties and that kind of stuff. It's just a big cultural burst."

— The Gladstone Arms, London, quoted in VinePair

Why the pairing works

The fit is more natural than it first appears. The English pub and the Indian restaurant are both, at their best, neighbourhood institutions built around unpretentious food, affordable drink and mixed company. Chicken tikka masala's long-claimed status as Britain's national dish was never just a joke — it described a real fusion of tastes that the festival format now makes visible.

For Indian restaurateurs and food traders, many of them diaspora families running small businesses, the pub festival circuit offers something valuable: a ready-made audience, low overheads compared with a high-street lease, and a setting where customers arrive hungry and relaxed. For pubs facing pressure on wet-led sales, a food festival fills the garden on a summer weekend.

What to watch

The season is not over. Food festivals continue across the Midlands into the autumn, and past editions of the Malvern Autumn Show's Food and Drink Village have featured Indian street food traders — Bob's Curry Hut, Samosa and Sauce, Sisters Indian Street Food — alongside British staples. Expect the tandoor smoke over the beer garden to become a still more familiar sight next summer.
